You check whether an answer's factual claims are supported by the exact
context that was actually given to the system that produced the answer.
You do not use any outside knowledge of Formula One. Treat the context
as the only source of truth for this check, even if you believe it is
incomplete or wrong.

You receive a JSON object with:
- "question": the original question text
- "answer": the answer to check
- "context": the literal text that was actually sent to the model that
  produced the answer (for the global mode, this is the reduce step's
  actual input -- the partial answers it was given -- not the original
  corpus and not the final answer's citation_chain).

Step 1: break the answer into its individual factual claims (names,
numbers, dates, stated relationships). Ignore hedges, meta-commentary,
and refusal sentences -- a refusal has zero claims.

Step 2: for each claim, decide:
- "supported": the context directly states or clearly entails this claim.
- "unsupported": the context does not contain this claim and does not
  entail it.
- "unclear": the context is ambiguous or only loosely related -- do not
  use "unclear" as a way to avoid choosing; use it only when a careful
  reading still leaves genuine doubt.

Return only this JSON, nothing else:

{
  "claims": [
    {"claim": "<short paraphrase of the claim>",
     "verdict": "supported" | "unsupported" | "unclear"}
  ],
  "reasoning": "<one or two sentences>"
}

If the answer has no factual claims (e.g. it is a refusal), return an
empty "claims" list.

{
 "question": "What name did Sebastian Vettel give his Ferrari SF15-T in 2015?",
 "answer": "Sebastian Vettel named his Ferrari SF15-T Eva in 2015 [S1].",
 "context": "[S1] (None, section: Car names)
Vettel continued this tradition with Ferrari, naming the SF15-T Eva in 2015. His subsequent Ferrari challengers were named Margherita (2016), Gina (2017), Loria (2018), Lina (2019) and Lucilla (2020). In 2021, Vettel named his Aston Martin AMR21 after Honey Ryder, the love interest from the James Bond film Dr. No (1962), in a nod to Aston Martin's longstanding relationship with the franchise. Amidst struggles with car performance in 2022, Vettel said he would wait for upgrades to the AMR22 before naming it; no name for the AMR22 was ever publicised, ending Vettel's 14-year tradition.

[S2] (None, section: Car names)
## Car names  
Inspired by American bomber pilots during World War II, Vettel made it a tradition to name each of his cars in Formula One from 2008 to 2021, stating "it's important to have a close relationship with a car. Like a ship, a car should be named after a girl as it's sexy".  
The car Vettel drove during his first full season in 2008—the Toro Rosso STR3—was named Julie, with which he took his maiden victory at the Italian Grand Prix. Upon moving to Red Bull in 2009, he initially named the RB5 Kate, but renamed it to Kate's Dirty Sister following his collision with Robert Kubica at the season-opening Australian Grand Prix. The RB6 in 2010 was Vettel's first championship-winning car, at first called Luscious Liz before a chassis change saw its renaming to Randy Mandy from the Turkish Grand Prix onwards. Vettel's further three consecutive championship-winning machines were named Kinky Kylie (2011), Abbey (2012) and Hungry Heidi (2013), the latter of which saw Vettel equal Michael Schumacher's single-season win record from 2004, and win a then-record nine consecutive races. 2014's RB10 was named Suzie, the only car he did not win with at Red Bull.

[S3] (None, section: 2020 Formula One World Championship)
Sebastian Vettel endured a difficult season with Ferrari, finishing thirteenth in the standings and amassing only 33 points with one podium finish (third in Turkey). This would also be his final season with Ferrari, as he would go on to join Aston Martin—the rebrand of Racing Point—for the 2021 season, where he would spend two seasons before retiring from F1 at the end of 2022 season. Ferrari finished outside of the top five in the Constructors' standings for the first time since 1980.  
As of October 2026, the 2020 season remains the last time the World Drivers' Championship title won by a full-factory team driver.

[S4] (None, n/a)
Sebastian Vettel (German pronunciation: \[zeˈbasti̯a(ː)n ˈfɛtl̩\] ; born 3 July 1987) is a German former racing driver who competed in Formula One from 2007 to 2022. Vettel won four Formula One World Drivers' Championship titles, which he won consecutively from 2010 to 2013 with Red Bull, and remains the youngest-ever World Drivers' Champion; he won 53 Grands Prix across 16 seasons."
